To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the sleep-time produced in HS mice by pentobarbital and ethanol are not correlated; (2) the sensitivity of HS mice to ethanol is related to the sensitivity of the brain membranes to ethanol and flunitrazepan, but not to pentabarbitol, and (3) muscimol stimulation of chloride uptake in brain membranes from HS mice is not related to ethanol sensitivity.
the sensitivity to ethanol and pentobarbitals does not cosegregate in genetically heterogeneous mice.

sensitivity to ethanol hypnosis does not cosegregate in HS mice with sensitivity to pentobarbitaI hypnosis and that muscimol-sensitive chloride uptake is differentially modulated by ethanol and flunitrazepam, but not by pentobarbital in brain membranes from HS mice.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the genetic mechanisms of ethanol-induced sleepiness.
the genetic and molecular basis of the sedative action of alcohol and barbiturates.
the identification of the genetic factors which determine individual differences in sensitivity to ethanol.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the data are consistent with the hypothesis that the sedative effects of ethanol and barbiturates may be mediated by separate mechanisms.
the data are not consistent with the hypothesis that the sedative effect of ethanol is genetically linked to the effect of pentobarbalt on GABAA receptors.
the genetic basis for sensitivity to ethanol-induced sedation is not linked to the genetic basis for sedation by barbiturates or benzodiazepines.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the genetic basis for sensitivity to ethanol is different from that for sensitivity to barbiturates.
sensitivity to pentobarbatal, ethanol and flunitrazapam are not linked.
ethanol, pentobarbitol, and flunitrezapam may act on the GABA-A receptor complex, and that the effects of these agents may be related, but that they may not be mediated by the same genetic mechanism.
The main takeaway from our work is that
sensitivity to ethanol does not cosegregate (or correlate) with sensitivity to pentobarbatal.
sensitivity to ethanol and sensitivity to pentobarbatal are not genetically linked in mice.
there are multiple mechanisms for the effects of alcohol and barbiturates on sleep.
